name: Daria Wagner

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time, Daria. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not linked to any company, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I mind a row of twelve sock knitting machines at Ashworth Hosiery, an old mill that's been in the town since my gran's time. Each machine knits a sock tube in about two minutes, and I keep them fed with yarn cones, mend dropped stitches and pull out any sock with a hole. When a needle snaps, I'm supposed to change it myself, but I'm still slow, so I often call Maureen, the senior knitter.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Who do you live with, and how are things with money?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the hum of the room and the women I work with. Some of them knew my gran. The hard bit is my eyes by the end of the shift, from staring at tiny stitches. I've used an AI app a few times, for recipes and once to write a letter to the council, but never at work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, maybe now people will stop going on about it. At church I'd say we've got enough to worry about without robots. I wouldn't post anything, I'm not one for that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, we went on short weeks twice last year when a big shop changed suppliers. The mill's real problem is cheap socks from abroad, not AI. That worry doesn't go anywhere just because the robots didn't come.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and get quicker at changing needles, so I'm not leaning on Maureen. Mark and I would keep saving for the wedding, we've got about three months of bills put by. I'd pick up Saturday shifts whenever they're offered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relieved, but not easy. The mill has always felt one bad order from trouble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Mark do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mark, my boyfriend, is in his last year of a plumbing apprenticeship. Once he qualifies, his pay goes up a fair bit. Until then, my wage is the steadier one, which is a bit funny given the mill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would short weeks mean for you two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd stop putting money in the wedding pot and just cover the rent. It happened last spring, and we didn't go out for six weeks. We managed, but it wasn't nice.

say: I'd say good, maybe now people will **stop going on** about it.
At church I'd say we have **enough to worry about** already.
think: Privately, the mill's real problem is **cheap imported socks**, not AI.
We went on **short weeks twice** last year when a shop changed suppliers.
do: Get quicker at **changing needles** so I'm not leaning on Maureen.
Keep saving **for the wedding** with three months of bills put by.
Pick up **Saturday shifts** whenever they're offered.
feel: Relieved, but **not easy**, as the mill is always one bad order from trouble.
S0.quote: The mill's real problem is cheap socks from abroad, not AI. That worry doesn't go anywhere just because the robots didn't come.
fieldNote: Her steady worry is **imports and short weeks**, which AI Plateau leaves untouched.
For now **her wage is steadier** than her boyfriend's apprentice pay.
She leans on Maureen (a senior knitter) and **wants to stop**.

steps.text: Practise changing snapped needles without calling Maureen
Keep paying into the wedding pot each month
Take every Saturday shift the mill offers

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the office jobs that'll go first, and maybe that's no bad thing, there are too many managers. At the mill I'd say we're fine for now. I'd say it a bit too confidently.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think Ashworth would use it to cut the office and then look hard at us. The new knitting machines can already change their own needles and sort bad socks with a camera. If the mill buys a few of the new knitting machines, they don't need twelve machines per person. They need one person for forty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Maureen to teach me the newer machines in the corner, because those are the ones they'll keep. I'd try the AI app for the mill's new stock system once the others are using it. And Mark and I would push the wedding back a few months to build the savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not panicking, but I'd lie awake sometimes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at the mill would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maureen, oddly, even though she's the best. She's sixty-one and she won't want to learn a camera system. If they offered her early retirement, I think she'd take it, and I'd miss her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you blame if jobs go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The big shops that only care about the cheapest price, and people who buy six socks for a pound. If people bought proper socks made here, the mill would be fine. I don't blame the robots, they're just a tool.

At the mill I'd say **we're fine**, a bit too confidently.

Push **the wedding back** a few months to build savings.

fieldNote: She blames **cheap-price shops** and shoppers, not the robots.
Her steady style shows: she'll try AI **once others have**.
The wedding is the **first thing she'd delay** to protect savings.

steps.text: Learn the camera-equipped knitting machines from Maureen
Use the AI app for the mill's stock system once others do
Push the wedding back a few months
Put the wedding money into savings for now

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going too fast and it isn't right. At church people would say we need to look after each other, and I'd agree. I'd keep off the internet, it'd be full of nonsense.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, the mill's office and orders go to AI in 2028, and by 2031 the robots do my job. I'm junior and still slow on needles, so I'd go early. I think I'd be out by thirty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd postpone the wedding and put all the money into savings, aiming for six months. I'd ask Mark to finish his apprenticeship as fast as he can, because plumbing in people's houses is harder for robots. In the first year after AGI I'd look for work in a care home, where people need people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. My chest goes tight thinking about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the three-year gap before robots mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Three years to find something else while still getting paid at the mill. It's not much, but it's something. I'd rather have three years than none.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you two still have children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd want to, but not until one of us had steady work. My gran had my mum in a worse time than this, she always said. Maybe that's what I'd tell myself before having children.

say: I'd say it's going **too fast** and isn't right.
At church I'd say we need to **look after each other**.
think: Being **junior and slow** on needles, I'd be out by thirty.
do: **Postpone the wedding** and move the money into savings.
Encourage Mark (my boyfriend) to **finish his apprenticeship** fast.
Look for **care home work** in the first year after AGI.
S2.quote: My gran had my mum in a worse time than this, she always said. Maybe that's what I'd tell myself before having children.
fieldNote: She sees **Mark's plumbing** as the household's safer income.
Her faith and **family memory** steady her in the worst case.
She'd delay **the wedding and children** until work looks steady.

steps.text: Postpone the wedding until work looks steady
Move the wedding money into savings to reach six months
Apply for care assistant jobs at local care homes
Lean on Mark's plumbing pay once he qualifies

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a warning we should take seriously. At the mill I'd tell the younger girls to learn something extra. At church we'd probably start a jobs board.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, robots by 2034 still take the knitting, but by then Mark would be a qualified plumber, and I'd have time to get a care qualification. I'd be about thirty-five. It's frightening, but I can see us getting through.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd keep the wedding date and do a care certificate at the college on Saturday mornings. I'd keep working at the mill and save. I'd move to care work in two or three years, once I've got the certificate and Mark's qualified.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but not as bad as the fast one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why care work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My gran was in a home at the end, and the carers were lovely. You can't put a robot in charge of somebody's gran, or I hope you can't. It's also a proper job with people around you, like the mill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make it easier?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Courses that don't cost the earth, and employers that give you a proper apprenticeship. I'm not after handouts. I'm after a way to earn my keep.

do: Keep **the wedding date** and save from the mill wage.
Do a **care certificate** on Saturday mornings this year.
Move into **care work** in two or three years.

S3.quote: You can't put a robot in charge of somebody's gran, or I hope you can't.
fieldNote: Her choice of **care work** comes from her gran's last years.

steps.text: Take a care certificate at college on Saturday mornings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time and we'll manage. At the mill I'd tell people not to panic. At church I'd say the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, robots by 2039 still mean the mill goes, but I'd be thirty-nine and probably doing something else. Mark would have his own plumbing van by then, he hopes. We'd be all right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd have the wedding as planned next year and start thinking about children. I'd stay at the mill a few more years and do the care certificate when the time feels right. We'd save for a house deposit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, a little. Mostly it feels like a long way off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When would the time feel right for the care certificate?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: When I see the new machines actually come into the mill, probably. I'm not one to jump first. If Maureen's corner machines start doing everything, that's my sign.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a risk you'd leave it too late?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. Waiting for a sign is how I've always done things, and it's usually worked. But ten years makes it easy to wait too long.

As a household, I think we'd be **all right**.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd lose the mill job just when Mark and I want to marry and have children. What would help is cheap courses with proper apprenticeships, and a bit of time to change before the robots come.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about the old mills. When an old mill goes, it's not just jobs. It's the whole street, the café, the church hall.

headlineQuote: When an old mill goes, it's not just jobs. It's the whole street, the café, the church hall.
portrait: Daria is a **27-year-old knitting machine operator** at an old sock mill.
She lives with **Mark (her boyfriend)**, a plumbing apprentice, with three months saved.
She's **churchgoing and traditional**, blaming cheap-price shops rather than robots.
She tries AI only **once others have**, and would move into care work.
Her mood moves from uneasy to alarmed at **AGI by 2028**, tied to wedding and children.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, as it hits just as she wants to marry.
whatWouldHelp: **Cheap courses** with proper apprenticeships, and time to change.
